tactics.claim: Demonstrate rather than describe: lead with the product attribute whose result you can actually show working on camera or in frame, design the demonstration to be dramatic enough to produce a 'wow', and treat any attribute whose result cannot be shown as unsellable in a visual slot (relegate it to text). When a demonstration goes stale, shoot a bigger one rather than repeating it.
tactics.mechanism: A remote buyer who cannot see, touch or hold the product has no sense of ownership, so desire has to be created visually. A shown result is believed because the prospect draws the superiority conclusion themselves; an asserted one is discounted. A dramatic demonstration telegraphs the benefit faster than words can, while complex, invisible or prevention-based results have no demonstration available and never produce the 'wow' that stops a scroll.
tactics.evidence: Teardowns only, no conversion data: OxiClean stains disappearing on camera, Mighty Mend It repairing a flag that withstands hurricane-force winds, the DualSaw cutting a car in half, Billy holding a live skunk for an odor killer, dangling from the HMS Bounty for Mighty Putty, hitting his hand with a mallet for Impact Gel insoles; plus the negative case that prevention-based products 'never sell well' because there is no visible result, and the assertion that 'regular claims with heaps of evidence are not even a fraction as potent.'

tactics.claim: Sell the removal of a pain the buyer feels today rather than prevention of a problem they might face later — and if they do not yet perceive the problem, confront them with it before offering the solution.

Pain removal is easier to sell than progress toward a goal, and naming a problem the buyer has not consciously registered ('are you tired of knives that just don't cut?') creates the felt problem the offer then resolves.

tactics.claim: Put the product in the hands of real users in the hardest use case before you build any promotion — give free samples in exchange for honest opinions and what they would pay — and kill or fix the product if the feedback is not strong.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add offer sequencing: state the price early rather than at the end, and place value-stacking elements (bundle framing, free portion, guarantee, quantity argument) after the price on the page and in email — reconciled with the information-fatigue rule to order by decision-relevance.

tactics.claim: Immediately after stating the price, sweeten the deal — add bonus items with a stated dollar value ('as a special bonus we'll also include...'), and/or double or triple the quantity ('order right now and I'll send you a second one absolutely free, just pay shipping and processing') — then total the whole thing against the price so the value dwarfs the cost.
tactics.mechanism: Stacking additional value on a price the prospect has just heard builds momentum and turns indecisive prospects into buyers, because perceived value moves sharply while the price does not; the doubled quantity reads as an extraordinary deal at the same price point, and shipping-and-processing on the free unit recovers part of the landed cost.
tactics.evidence: Several stock phrasings plus the full Tool Band-It close ('two original tool bandits and our world famous Hercules hooks, a $50 value, for only $19.95', with the hooks framed as 'a $10 value') and the assertion that doubling 'is usually enough to push them over to the sales side'. Worked scripts, no performance data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable in principle but almost entirely duplicative of a rule already scored 8 and adopted for this catalogue, and the one non-duplicated variant is economically unsafe here.

tactics.rejectReason: marketing-offer-construction already owns buy-X-get-Y where the free units outnumber the paid ones (buy four get eight, not buy one get one, with unit price raised so the total holds), the rule that the same economics can be stated as percent off, dollars off, a free portion or a total package price with a value anchor, the named-bundle tier rule, the prefer-adding-good-stuff-over-cutting-price rule, and the '$1 add-on recovers landed cost' variant. The only element not explicitly owned — free plus shipping — is a near-variant of the splinter rule and a poor fit: at a $50.46 AOV with real COGS and postage, 'second stick free, just pay shipping' on a $12 consumable can go cash-negative per order, the exact failure the splinter rule already warns about. Adopting the weaker form would muddy a rule already scored 8/10.

tactics.claim: When the offer runs indefinitely and cannot carry a real expiry date, build urgency by attaching the bonus or extra unit to the act of ordering now ('order right now and I'll also send you...') rather than by claiming a deadline.
tactics.mechanism: Conditional phrasing ties the extra value to the action rather than to a calendar, so the reader feels they must act to get everything on the table, while the seller never asserts an expiry that will not actually happen — which is what a permanently-running ad or an evergreen listing cannot honestly do.
tactics.evidence: Observation only: Schefren notes that because the commercial ran continuously Billy 'couldn't have a time limit or an expiration date, but the way he described it made you feel that you needed to order now'. No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (urgency framing), so the 2009 date is irrelevant. It fills a genuine hole in marketing-scarcity-urgency-framing, which currently prescribes only real, honoured deadlines and seasonal re-wraps — but the two surfaces carrying most revenue cannot hold a deadline at all: an Amazon listing (~$1,800/mo) is evergreen and policy-constrained, and an always-on Shopify PDP has no countdown. The honest translation is conditional bonus phrasing on the PDP and in cart/post-purchase copy ('add the refill now and the lip balm ships with it'), with the hard guardrail that the offer must actually be attached to that order rather than implied to be expiring. Capped at 5 because the source's own version leans on manufactured feeling, that drift is exactly what the existing skill's 'the deadline must be genuinely honored' rule prohibits, and at ~54 orders/month the effect will be judged, never measured.

targetSkill.name: marketing-scarcity-urgency-framing
targetSkill.description: Add deadline-free urgency for evergreen surfaces: attach a bonus or extra unit conditionally to this order ('add it now and it ships with your order') on the PDP, cart and post-purchase copy, with the guardrail that the condition must be real and no expiry may be implied.

tactics.claim: Eliminate the buyer's perceived risk with a money-back guarantee, because remote buyers cannot see, touch or try the product and are otherwise being asked to carry all the risk themselves; refunds will be a small fraction of the incremental sales.
tactics.mechanism: Every purchase decision carries risk, and distance selling amplifies it; if the seller genuinely believes in the product they should bear that risk, and removing it from the buyer's side lifts conversion by more than the refunds cost.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only — 'sales always go up', with no figures, no refund rates and no named cases.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (offer construction), age irrelevant — rejected for duplication, not staleness.

tactics.rejectReason: marketing-offer-construction already owns risk reversal in a more specific and better-calibrated form for this business (name the buyer's single biggest fear, go broad and unconditional at low-ticket B2C, build the cost into the price, place the promise next to add-to-cart rather than in the footer), and marketing-conversion-friction-audit owns making return and guarantee terms visible on the page. Nothing here is additive at a $50.46 AOV.

tactics.claim: Close with an unhedged direct command — 'order right now', 'call now' — repeated through the back half of the pitch rather than softening the ask (the veteran pitchmen's 'chill-down'), and pair it with taking the risk off the buyer's shoulders.
tactics.mechanism: Once the pain has been surfaced, the product demonstrated, the alternatives contrasted, the offer sweetened and the risk reversed, the only step left is to tell the reader exactly what to do; a timid or hedged ask leaves a persuaded reader with no instruction to act on and lets momentum dissipate, while the authoritative tone signals the seller's own belief in the product.
tactics.evidence: Two phrases pulled from Billy Mays' pitches plus the Zig Ziglar line 'timid salespeople have skinny kids'. Assertion only, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (copy craft), age irrelevant. Narrowly additive: marketing-email-design-production owns CTA placement and bridging the ask to what was just read, and marketing-conversion-copy-angles owns register and pronouns, but nothing owns the ask being an unhedged imperative repeated after the argument lands — the exact failure mode of a solo operator drafting with an LLM, since brand prose defaults to 'you can learn more here'. Free, editorial, applies to the Shopify PDP CTA, the post-purchase and reorder emails where the 18–22.5% repeat rate is decided, and Meta primary text on the $30/day giveaway campaign ('enter now' rather than 'buy now'). Capped at 5 because it is a one-line craft habit rather than a revenue mechanism, it is close kin to CTA rules already recorded, it must be scoped away from Amazon A+ content where cart-directing language is policy-constrained, and at ~54 orders/month no version of the sentence will ever be measurably better. The risk-reversal half of the source's pairing is not additive — the guarantee rule in marketing-offer-construction and the urgency rules in marketing-scarcity-urgency-framing already cover it, and bare 'order now' pressure with no expiring thing behind it is the empty version this catalogue has already ruled out.

targetSkill.name: marketing-conversion-copy-angles
targetSkill.description: Add an unhedged-imperative close: after the argument lands, state the ask as a direct command and repeat it, never as 'you can learn more here' — scoped to PDP CTAs, emails and ad primary text, and away from Amazon A+ content where cart-directing language is policy-constrained.

tactics.claim: Validate an offer on the smallest, cheapest audience that predicts the full result — kill it there if it does not pull, and only then roll out to expensive channels; Schefren's own version is to test every new product to the house email list first, and only if it beats expectations go out to affiliates, PPC and SEO.
tactics.mechanism: Direct response is trackable, so a cheap surface can predict a larger one; testing where the cost of a failure is smallest means most of the money and time gets spent riding winners rather than discovering losers at full price.
tactics.evidence: Billy and Sully's cheap predictive TV test markets, Joseph Sugarman testing every ad in the Southwestern edition of the Wall Street Journal, and Schefren's own stated house-list-first sequence. Practitioner anecdotes, no figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (test ordering), age irrelevant. Additive on a different axis from the rules already recorded: marketing-awareness-level-messaging's cheap-reversible-first rule orders copy angles (ad text before PDP rebuild), while this orders audiences — validate a new bundle, price or promotion by emailing the owned list before putting any of the $30/day Meta budget or Amazon listing changes behind it. Free, needs no attribution (redemption reads off a discount code), and it is the natural companion to the existing 'run the price escalation on Shopify first, not Amazon' rule, since Amazon changes are slow to unwind on the larger ~$1,800/mo channel. Capped at 5 because it substantially overlaps those two rules, and because the source's stop-rule does not survive the scale-down: at a sub-1,000 subscriber list and ~54 orders/month, 'sales were disappointing, kill it' is a directional judgement on a handful of orders, so treat a flat list test as a reason not to fund it yet, never as proof the offer is dead.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add an audience test-order rule: validate a new bundle, price or promotion on the owned email list first (redemption tracked by discount code) before funding it with paid media or slow-to-unwind Amazon listing changes — with the caveat that at this order volume a flat list test is a reason not to fund yet, not proof the offer is dead.

tactics.claim: Strive to be the best in the world at the one thing you do, because 'if you're the best in the world, the phone rings' — Billy started selling washing machines on a boardwalk and refined his method over years of commission-only feedback.
tactics.mechanism: Excellence in a single narrow skill creates inbound demand, and that excellence is built through years of high-feedback repetition rather than arriving fully formed.
tactics.evidence: Biographical narrative of Billy Mays' career plus a Seth Godin quote. Motivational framing, no testable procedure.

rscFit.reasoning: No stated mechanism a solo operator could execute or test — no artifact, surface or decision attached.

tactics.rejectReason: Motivational framing with no procedure, and no honest translation to an ecommerce catalogue at any size: 'the phone rings' is a service/talent model, not a mechanism for selling a $12 deodorant.
